metadata.title: Asset Metadata Cache Tasks
metadata.description: A local SQLite asset metadata cache in the Electron main process that resolves tickers, names and decimal places from the Cardano token registry, applies decimal places only when the metadata is cryptographically bound to the minting policy, adds CIP-25 and CIP-68 names through a Koios pointer the user's own node confirms, and removes the one-minute poll of the wallet assets endpoint
metadata.importantNote: verified must mean the whole chain passed: the policy field hashes to the subject's policy id, the script requires the key hash of the signing public key, and the ed25519 signature over the attestation payload verifies. It must not mean that the server returned a signature, which would collapse back to trusting the operator. task-019 must not ship if task-009's corpus gate was not met. No cardano-wallet change is in scope: the wallet keeps its --token-metadata-server wiring at source/main/index.ts:215-218 and this design simply stops exercising it. Koios is adopted as the pointer service for on-chain metadata (PRD locked decision 9) and it is ADDITIVE to tokens.cardano.org, never a replacement (locked decision 10): Koios strips the registry signatures, returning bare name, description, ticker, url, logo and decimals with no policy, no sequenceNumber and no signatures, so every input to the verification chain is absent from it. Verified decimal places keep coming direct from tokens.cardano.org, and a chain-sourced row leaves decimals NULL so no amount anywhere is formatted by a number that came from Koios. The metadata source is user-selectable in the shape SMASH already uses (locked decision 11): the Koios preset and the custom URL ship together in phase 7, and the direct option is carried in the enum and rendered unavailable until the local scan machinery exists.

phases.name: Standalone Correctness Fixes
phases.description: Everything that improves what the user sees without a cache, an IPC channel or a new dependency. Four independent commits, each revertible alone, each shippable before the rest of the plan exists.

tasks.title: Resolve asset names by provenance and stop rendering non-text as text
tasks.description: components/assets/Asset.tsx:177-178 renders `ASCII: ${hexToString(assetName)}` whenever there is no metadata name. hexToString is Buffer.from(hex,'hex').toString() (utils/strings.ts:18-19), which decodes as UTF-8 unconditionally, so an asset whose name is a hash renders the literal prefix followed by replacement characters. Add a printable-ASCII predicate and a resolution order, and drop the prefix.
implementationNotes: Resolution order, highest first: registry ticker, registry name, the CIP-25 or CIP-68 name the chain channel resolves in task-035, decoded asset name when printable, nothing. Until the cache lands the first three are simply absent, so this task is the fourth rung and the ordering it sits in.
The predicate is: decode asset_name from hex, accept only if every resulting byte is in 0x20 to 0x7E inclusive. Reject the empty name.

Do not simply delete the 'ASCII: ' prefix. Today it is the only thing marking the decoded bytes as raw asset-name bytes rather than a name an issuer published. Asset names are chosen freely by whoever mints, so an asset whose name bytes spell USDC would otherwise render into the same displayName span as a genuine registry USDC, separable only by the fingerprint. Replace the prefix with a visually distinct treatment for a minter-chosen decoded name, on every surface that renders a name. The exact treatment is a design decision; the requirement is that a user can tell a decoded name from a published one without reading the fingerprint. styles.ascii at Asset.tsx:209 is a starting point.
The fingerprint is rendered separately at Asset.tsx:199-203 and remains the identity when no name resolves. Do not substitute a truncated policy id.
domains/Asset.ts:22-25 already exposes assetNameASCII as a MobX computed over the same bytes. Put the predicate beside it rather than duplicating the decode.
testCases: A printable name renders decoded and without a prefix
A 32-byte random asset name renders no name at all, only the fingerprint
An empty asset name renders no name
A name whose bytes are valid UTF-8 but outside ASCII renders no name, which is the conservative choice recorded in the PRD
acceptance: A minter-chosen decoded name renders in a treatment visually distinct from a registry or CIP-25 name, on the token list, the send form and the transaction list
An asset whose name bytes spell an existing registry ticker is distinguishable from the real one without reading the fingerprint, demonstrated with a fixture for both
No token row in the list or the send form shows replacement characters
The predicate rejects the empty name and any byte outside 0x20 to 0x7E, asserted per boundary
yarn lint, yarn compile and yarn test:jest pass
tasks.notes: The marking is a security requirement, not a cosmetic one, and it is what the CIP-30 connector's 'display problem rather than an impersonation one' assumption rests on.

A token with no cached metadata therefore has no identity and is dropped. Under the current poll this is masked; with a cache that starts cold it empties the send form, the send confirmation and the transaction list.

Overlay only the lookup fields that exist
Delete the .filter((token) => !!token.uniqueId) in getNonZeroAssetTokens, which then has nothing left to remove

The fingerprint sort inside getNonZeroAssetTokens is unchanged. WalletSummaryPage.tsx:123-125 re-sorts afterward, so the two orders do not conflict.

A token whose subject has a cached row gains decimals and metadata and keeps its own quantity and address

tasks.title: Stop the amount field accepting a decimal separator when decimal places are unknown
tasks.description: components/wallet/send-form/AssetInput.tsx:116 passes decimalPlaces={decimals}, and decimals is undefined for every asset the user has never configured (domains/Asset.ts:18). With decimalPlaces undefined the react-polymorph NumericInput accepts a decimal separator, and WalletSendForm.tsx:235 then strips it with formattedAmountToNaturalUnits (utils/formatters.ts:163-167), so entering 1.5 produces a natural-unit amount of 15. On the Cardano ledger every quantity is an integer and decimal places are presentation only, so raw units are the correct display for an asset whose decimals are unknown and a separator typed into that field is meaningless input. Make the input path consistent with the confirmation dialog, which already shows both representations honestly.
implementationNotes: Pass allowOnlyIntegers to the NumericInput whenever the resolved decimal places are unknown. node_modules/react-polymorph/lib/components/NumericInput.js:197 and :199 select an integers-only input pattern from it, so the separator cannot be typed or pasted.

Label the field with the token's ticker or fingerprint rather than the formatted-amount placeholder built at AssetInput.tsx:105-111, which currently renders '0' and implies an integer without saying so.
Delete the keypress guard at AssetInput.tsx:128-137. It fires only when decimals === 0 and is redundant once allowOnlyIntegers covers both the zero and the unknown case.

The defect is the asymmetry with the screen that follows. The send confirmation renders the formatted amount at containers/wallet/dialogs/send-confirmation/DialogContentWithAssets.tsx:75 and the raw amount at :109-110, under unformattedAmountLabel and the tooltip explaining the difference in the sibling messages.ts:87-98. The confirmation is honest about the two representations while the input converts one into the other by stripping a character.
Do not block and do not refuse. A user holding a token the registry has never heard of must still be able to spend it, and raw units are the units it is actually denominated in.

Measured in this tree, and the reason the defect is invisible: new BigNumber('1.23456789').toFixed(undefined, 4) returns '1.23456789' rather than throwing, and undefined > 0 is false, so NumericInput.js:285 and :319 take the branch that appends the separator to the displayed value.
testCases: With decimals undefined, typing a decimal separator into the asset amount field has no effect
With decimals undefined, pasting '1.5' yields the field value '15' or is rejected outright, and never a value the form then reinterprets
With decimals set to 6, the field still accepts '1.5' and yields 1500000 natural units
With decimals set to 0, behavior is unchanged from today
acceptance: yarn test:jest passes
The amount entered and the amount in the built transaction agree for every combination of decimals set, unset and zero
securityNotes: A live defect today and independent of the rest of the plan. It lands in the first phase because it is small, self-contained and revertible on its own, not because it is urgent.

Severity is bounded and should not be scheduled as an emergency. Decimal places are presentation only, so the realistic harm is a user who knows their token carries six decimals typing 1.5, meaning one and a half tokens, and sending 15 raw units: a large underpayment, not a tenfold overspend. The overspend direction appears at the migration in task-021, not here.

phases.name: The Main-Process Cache
phases.description: The database, the registry client, the verification chain and the resolver that sequences them, built and tested with no consumer. Verification carries the only real uncertainty in the plan and is gated on its own corpus check before anything depends on it.

tasks.title: Compute CIP-14 asset fingerprints locally
tasks.description: fingerprint is today a field of the assets endpoint response (api/assets/types.ts:18), so dropping that endpoint drops the only source of the identifier the token row renders most prominently (Asset.tsx:199-203). CIP-14 is computable from the policy id and the asset name with packages already in the tree.

logic: Concatenate the hex-decoded policy id and the hex-decoded asset name
Take blake2b-160 over the result using blake2b(20) from the blake2b package
Encode with bech32 using the human-readable part 'asset', via the bech32 package

implementationNotes: Both packages are already declared: blake2b at package.json:210 and bech32 at package.json:207. No new dependency.

Verified in this tree against the eight golden vectors in cardano-wallet at lib/primitive/test/spec/Cardano/Wallet/Primitive/Types/TokenFingerprintSpec.hs:40-78, including the empty asset name and the 32-byte asset name cases.
This lives in the renderer rather than main. It is a pure function of data the renderer already has, it must work with a cold cache, and putting it behind IPC would add a round trip to render a row.
testCases: All eight golden vectors from TokenFingerprintSpec.hs:40-78 produce their published fingerprints
An empty asset name produces a fingerprint rather than throwing
An odd-length or non-hex input is rejected
acceptance: yarn test:jest passes with all eight vectors asserted
No new entry in package.json
tasks.notes: Load-bearing, not an optimization. Without it the token row loses its identifier the moment the endpoint goes.

tasks.title: Database module: schema, open, version check, point read and write
tasks.description: A node:sqlite database under the state directory holding asset_metadata, asset_image and asset_resolution as specified in the PRD, with the CHECK constraints that make an inconsistent row unwritable.
implementationNotes: DatabaseSync from node:sqlite. Verified in this repository under Electron 41.3.0 on Node 24.15.0 with no flag and no experimental warning; the bundled engine is SQLite 3.51.3, and STRICT tables, CHECK constraints and PRAGMA foreign_keys are all enforced.

Path: path.join(stateDirectoryPath, 'asset-metadata-cache', 'assets.sqlite'), with stateDirectoryPath from source/main/config.ts:125. Mirror anchorCacheDirectoryPath at source/main/governance/anchorCache.ts:36-37, including giving the database its own directory so the WAL and shared-memory siblings are contained.
Set PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL and PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON on open.
Check PRAGMA user_version on open. A file written by a newer version than the running code is deleted and recreated, not read: it holds nothing that cannot be fetched again.
Wrap every open, read and write so that a corrupt or unreadable file degrades to an empty cache rather than failing startup. anchorCache.ts:42-49 is the shape.

The primary key is the subject, and asset_resolution is keyed the same way, because what is cached is a property of the asset and not of the wallet holding it. Under the poll being removed, five wallets holding one token produce five fetches a minute for the same subject, roughly 7,200 a day for that one asset, since nothing between the store and the registry deduplicates by subject (AssetsStore.ts:13 and :157-170; cardano-wallet TokenMetadata.hs holds no IORef, TVar, MVar or memo structure). A subject-keyed table dissolves that by construction: one row and one resolution attempt however many wallets are open. A wallet-scoped backoff would retry a known-failing subject once per wallet and then wait out that many separate intervals.
Expose point reads keyed on subject and a batched upsert. Do not expose a full-table scan; nothing in the design enumerates the cache.

asset_metadata gains CHECK (decimals IS NULL OR (decimals >= 0 AND decimals <= 20)); assetsConfig.ts:1 sets MAX_DECIMAL_PRECISION = 20 and cardano-wallet accepts 0 to 255, so a verified value above 20 would otherwise be applied automatically while remaining unselectable in the dialog.
asset_resolution gains a state column with CHECK (state IN ('pending','resolved','unregistered','failed')), so a subject the registry silently omits is recorded rather than re-asked forever.
testCases: A row claiming both a sequence_number and a slot is rejected by the CHECK constraints
A row whose subject is not policy_id || asset_name is rejected
A verified value outside 0 and 1 is rejected
Opening a database whose user_version is ahead recreates it empty
Opening a truncated file recreates it empty rather than throwing
acceptance: yarn test:jest passes against a temporary database file
Deleting the directory while the process is running and reopening produces a working empty cache
A decimals value of 21 is rejected by the engine, asserted directly rather than by inspection
asset_resolution records state for every attempt outcome, including the 'unregistered' case where the batch succeeded and the subject was omitted

tasks.title: Registry client: batch query, timeout, retry and backoff
tasks.description: POST {metadataUrl}/metadata/query against the host named by launcherConfig.metadataUrl, with the same literal fallback already used at source/main/index.ts:217. Batched, sequential, timed out, and with a recorded retry-after on failure rather than a loop.
implementationNotes: Read the host from launcherConfig.metadataUrl (source/main/config.ts:71, populated per network at nix/internal/launcher-config.nix:37-41). Using the launcher value keeps the selfnode and testnet setups working, including the bundled mock-token-metadata-server, without a second configuration surface. Resolve the endpoint as launcherConfig.metadataUrl, then the configured source setting, then the bundled mock when network === 'selfnode', then the mainnet literal. launcher-config.nix:448-450 assigns metadataUrl under lib.optionalAttrs (network != 'selfnode'), so on selfnode the key is absent and the bare literal fallback would point at mainnet instead of the mock. The failure is silent, because a mainnet registry answers plausibly.
Request properties: name, ticker, decimals, url, description. Do not request logo. That is the 36 KiB field and it is fetched one subject at a time in task-011.

The response carries policy whether or not it is requested, which is what makes verification possible from the bulk query alone. Confirmed live on 2026-09-10 for subject c76ef5451f551f3c06d48c46b153cb35221b507683b2e413122661b942544544.

Size each batch by serialized request body bytes with a 6 KB ceiling, not by subject count. The endpoint caps the body near 8,192 bytes: measured 2026-09-14, 100 subjects at 7,892 bytes returned 200 and 110 at 8,614 returned 413, and two of eight sampled 100-subject batches failed on asset name length alone. A subject is 56 hex characters of policy id plus up to 64 of asset name, so 100 worst-case subjects is about 12.3 KB and always fails. Issue batches one after another rather than in parallel.

10 second timeout per request, matching ANCHOR_TIMEOUT_MS at source/main/governance/AnchorFetchService.ts:9. One retry after a short backoff, then abandon the batch and write an asset_resolution row whose retry_after doubles per consecutive failure up to a ceiling.
Cap the response body in bytes, as AnchorFetchService does, so a misbehaving host cannot exhaust memory.
The host is fixed and known, so the address-range filtering AnchorFetchService performs is not needed here. Do not copy it.
Log failures at debug without the subject list.
A 4xx is deterministic and is never retried. A 413 splits the batch once and re-sends; anything else 4xx is logged at warn with the body size and subject count, never the subject list.

The registry omits unknown subjects rather than returning a negative, so a batch that returns fewer entries than it asked for is a success. Write every omitted subject to asset_resolution in state 'unregistered', or NFT-holding wallets re-ask forever and the poll this plan deletes comes back.
testCases: A batch larger than the cap is split and issued sequentially
A request that exceeds the timeout is abandoned and records a retry-after
Consecutive failures lengthen the retry-after up to the ceiling and no further
A response over the byte cap is discarded
acceptance: A batch is sized by serialized request body bytes with a ceiling of 6 KB, and a unit test with 100 maximum-length subjects produces more than one batch
A 413 response splits the batch once and re-sends; a second 413 is recorded without a retry
No 4xx is ever scheduled for retry, asserted per status code
Subjects present in a request but absent from a 200 response are written to asset_resolution in state 'unregistered', asserted against a stub that omits one of two subjects
No timer anywhere in the module schedules unsolicited work
yarn test:jest passes against a stubbed transport
On selfnode the client resolves to the bundled mock-token-metadata-server and not to tokens.cardano.org, asserted by a manual QA case

tasks.title: Verification steps one and two: policy binding and key binding
tasks.description: Decode the policy field into a native script, prove that the script hashes to the subject's policy id, and prove that the script requires the key hash of the public key that signed the property under consideration.
implementationNotes: Step one: strip the two leading bytes from the policy field and take blake2b-224 over 0x00 concatenated with the remainder. The digest must equal the subject's first 28 bytes.
Step two: decode the native script and collect the key hashes it requires, then confirm that blake2b-224 of the signing publicKey is among them. A script that requires no key hash fails.

Both steps were reproduced locally against the live-captured subject with blake2b alone. The policy field 820182018282051a0303eb448200581c39a1df51147b6de6689a4727846962fb6540c3a3c7859a1a79b9420f yields policy id c76ef5451f551f3c06d48c46b153cb35221b507683b2e413122661b9, and public key 5817526d712f71e33a31ac3429fb7ce70b3e17e727044d9a2a51493e7894ba48 yields key hash 39a1df51147b6de6689a4727846962fb6540c3a3c7859a1a79b9420f, which the script requires.
blake2b(28) from the blake2b package gives the 224-bit digest. The package is already imported in the main process at source/main/governance/AnchorVerificationService.ts:1.
A subject with no policy field fails step one and is written with verified = 0. It is not an error and is not logged as one: it is the ordinary state of a large share of the registry.
Handle nested script forms. A policy that is an all, any or at-least combinator over sub-scripts requires walking it, and a signature from a key inside a satisfiable branch counts.
testCases: The live-captured subject passes both steps
A subject whose policy field hashes to a different policy id fails step one
A subject with no policy field fails step one
A signature from a key the script does not require fails step two
A nested all-of and any-of script resolves its key hashes correctly
acceptance: Policy binding: a fixture whose policy field digests to a different policy id returns false, and the failure names which digest differed
Script evaluation follows evaluatePolicy: all, any and atLeast are each covered by a fixture, including an atLeast(2 of 3) satisfied by one key, which must return false
Time-lock nodes evaluate to true regardless of the current clock, asserted with a policy whose lock expired in 2022
No path through the module can return true without both the policy digest and the script evaluation having been performed
yarn test:jest passes
securityNotes: verified is the output of this module and its successor. No field of the registry response may set it, directly or by default.

tasks.title: Verification step three: the attestation payload and ed25519, gated on the corpus
tasks.description: Verify the ed25519 signature over the registry's attestation payload for a property, sequence number included. The exact payload construction is read from the registry's own implementation rather than re-derived, and the module is not accepted until it verifies the full policy-bound corpus with zero failures.
implementationNotes: Verification uses Node's built-in crypto.verify(null, message, keyObject, signature) over an ed25519 raw public key, which adds nothing to the dependency tree. It is strict: tested 2026-09-14 against a real registry signature with its scalar S replaced by S + L, Node rejects it where cardano-crypto.js accepts it, so cardano-crypto.js is not used for this.

Take the payload construction from the registry's own implementation. A local sweep of 3,600 plausible constructions against a real mainnet subject did not reproduce the signature, which is why this is read rather than guessed.

The corpus gate: run verification over the full registry corpus and require zero failures across the policy-bound subjects before this task is accepted. This is not a CI check and not a unit test. It is a one-off validation whose result is recorded on the branch.

If Node's verifier turns out not to be strict enough on some platform build, promote @noble/curves from a transitive dependency (present at 1.9.7 through @trezor and @ethereumjs) to a declared one and use its ed25519, which rejected the same malleable signature. The primitive sits behind this module, so nothing else changes.
Verify each property independently. A subject may carry a verified ticker and an unverified decimals, and the row records the outcome per property rather than one verdict for the entry.
testCases: A tampered property value fails
A tampered sequence number fails
A signature valid for a different property of the same subject fails
A signature valid for the same property of a different subject fails
The live-captured subject's decimals property verifies
acceptance: The attestation payload is the 32-byte blake2b256 over the concatenated blake2b256 digests of CBOR(subject), CBOR(propertyName), CBOR(value) and CBOR(sequenceNumber), asserted against five live properties of a known subject
Verification uses Node's built-in crypto.verify, and a signature with S replaced by S + L is rejected, asserted directly
No new runtime dependency is added; package.json is unchanged by this task
The full policy-bound corpus verifies with zero failures
yarn test:jest passes
securityNotes: This is the step that makes verified mean something. If it is weakened, the decimals resolution order in phase 4 must not ship.

tasks.title: Resolver: sequence cache read, fetch, verify and write
tasks.description: The one module that owns the order of operations. It answers from the database, schedules what is missing, fetches in batches, verifies before writing, and emits the rows that resolved.
implementationNotes: Answer immediately from the database. Never wait on the network to satisfy a read.
Subtract the subjects that already have rows and the subjects whose asset_resolution retry_after has not elapsed, then batch the remainder.
Write verified = 1 only when every step of the chain passed for the property being written. Compute it here; never carry it from the response.
Emit resolved rows through a callback the IPC layer supplies. The resolver does not know about channels.
Do not hold the database open across a network call. Fetch, then verify, then write.
Offline is not an error condition. The fetch fails, the cache answers from disk, absent rows stay absent, and nothing is surfaced to the user.
No interval timer. Resolution is demand-driven, which is the entire point of removing the poll in task-018.

A row older than seven days is re-read on the next demand for it, never on a timer. The window is set from measurement, not assumption: of 7,976 registry mapping files at commit c9cf09f4, 7,464 (93.58 percent) sit at sequenceNumber 0 on every property, and in the last 365 days 375 commits touched mappings/ while only 38 files were modified rather than added. That is about one change somewhere in the registry every 9.6 days and a 0.48 percent per-asset annual change probability.

A refresh compares each property's sequenceNumber against the stored one and rewrites the row only when one has risen. updated_at is stamped on every successful read whether or not anything changed, which is what stops a never-updated subject from being re-read on every render.

The miss path is the one to engineer carefully and the refresh path is close to a formality. 375 commits against 38 modifications says the live event is a user acquiring a token the cache has never seen, not a record changing under one they already hold. Spend the effort on batching, backoff and correct rendering while a miss is outstanding.

The corpus rate is an average and does not apply directly. Assets a real user holds skew toward active projects and are likelier than average to update, so the real rate for held assets is above 0.48 percent and nobody has measured how far above. Do not present seven days as derived from the held-asset rate.
testCases: A read for a cached subject returns without touching the transport
A read for an uncached subject returns absent and schedules a fetch
A subject inside its retry-after window is not refetched
A response that fails verification is written with verified = 0 and not retried immediately
With the transport unavailable, reads still answer from disk
A row younger than the refresh window is answered from disk without a fetch
A row older than the refresh window is re-read on demand, and is rewritten only when a sequenceNumber has risen
acceptance: yarn test:jest passes against a stubbed transport and a temporary database
No setInterval or setTimeout schedules unsolicited work

tasks.title: Image store and its on-demand fetch
tasks.description: Registry logos are inline base64 PNG with a median entry of 36,191 bytes and 316 MiB across the corpus. They are fetched one subject at a time, only for assets the user holds, and only when something has decided to render one.
implementationNotes: A single-subject query requesting only the logo property. The bulk query in task-007 never requests it, which is what bounds the volume at the transport rather than only in the store.
Decode the base64 into a BLOB rather than storing the encoded string. Verified in this tree that node:sqlite round-trips a BLOB as a Uint8Array.
Discard any single entry over 256 KiB rather than storing it.
Record media_type from the payload and reject anything that is not an image type.
Never bulk mirror. There is no code path that enumerates subjects to warm this table.
testCases: An entry over the per-entry cap is discarded and the subject records no image
A non-image media type is rejected
A stored entry round-trips byte for byte
acceptance: yarn test:jest passes
The bulk query in task-007 still does not request the logo property

tasks.title: Image eviction under two bounds
tasks.description: At most 2,000 entries and at most 64 MiB in asset_image, evicting the least recently fetched, in the shape already used for DRep anchors at source/main/governance/anchorCache.ts:24-25.
implementationNotes: Both bounds, not one. At the 36 KiB median entry size they bite at roughly the same point, which is the intent: neither bound alone protects against the other's pathological case.
Order by fetched_at, which asset_image_fetched_at indexes. Update fetched_at on read so the ordering means least recently used rather than least recently written.
Eviction touches asset_image only. A row in asset_metadata carrying verified decimals must never be lost because a logo was evicted, which is why the two tables are separate.
testCases: Exceeding the entry bound evicts the oldest first
Exceeding the byte bound evicts until it is satisfied
Eviction leaves the corresponding asset_metadata rows untouched
acceptance: yarn test:jest passes
Neither bound can be exceeded after a write

phases.name: IPC And The Store
phases.description: Wire the cache to the renderer, rewire AssetsStore to read it, move the two call sites that enumerate the assets list, and only then remove the endpoint and the poll. The old source is taken away last, after the new one is proven to feed the store.

tasks.title: Declare the channels and the shared entry type
tasks.description: Three channel constants with their request and response types in source/common/ipc/api.ts, and the shared AssetMetadataEntry in a new source/common/types/asset-metadata.types.ts.
implementationNotes: ASSET_METADATA_CHANNEL is a renderer request for the rows the cache holds right now. It never waits on the network.
ASSET_METADATA_UPDATE_CHANNEL is the main-to-renderer push carrying rows as they resolve.
ASSET_IMAGE_CHANNEL is per subject, which is what keeps logos off the path of every other read.
Place them beside the governance block at source/common/ipc/api.ts:536-543 and follow its naming: RendererRequest and MainResponse for a request channel, MainRequest and RendererResponse for a push.
AssetMetadataEntry carries verified as a boolean and hasImage as a boolean. It does not carry the image bytes.

implementationNotes: The real mechanism is IpcChannel deriving three wire names from one base at source/common/ipc/lib/IpcChannel.ts:91-93: -broadcast, -request and -response. Nothing is ever sent on the bare constant.

send posts on -broadcast and pairs with onReceive; request posts on -request and pairs with onRequest. Mixing them sends to a name with no listener and neither side reports it, which is the failure a reader is most likely to hit and the document was silent on.
The two real ipcRenderer.send call sites are stores/WindowStore.ts:17 and :25, neither through a channel. Say so rather than deleting the mention.

The preload is not a hop. source/main/preload.ts:31 assigns ipcRenderer onto the renderer's global, which is what RendererIpcChannel defaults its sender and receiver to; nothing is forwarded through it.

IpcChannel<Incoming, Outgoing> is written from the declaring side's point of view, so the two sides list the same pair in the opposite order. The document had them the same on both sides, so a client copied from it has its types inside out.
Handlers are registered in source/main/ipc/index.ts, not source/main/index.ts.
The broadcast section described webContents.send on the bare constant, which appears nowhere in source/. The real push is channel.send(message, window.webContents).

Seven of the tabulated channels do not exist: the whole Cardano table. Twenty-four other names in those tables do. Replaced with the backend, watchdog, asset and governance channels that are declared.
Two snippets could not work: ipcMain.on('*'), because Electron has no wildcard channel, and a test mock of ipcRenderer.invoke, which nothing calls.

tasks.title: Confirm the pointer against the user's own chain before writing a row
tasks.description: Koios is read as an index, not an oracle. Before a chain-sourced row is written, the transaction the pointer names is read out of the user's own immutable database at block_hash and absolute_slot and checked to mint that asset under that policy and to carry that metadata. An index that lies fails the check; an index that is unreachable leaves the row absent.
implementationNotes: Three checks run against the tx_cbor bytes with no chain access at all, and all three were executed against a live response: blake2b-256 over the transaction body reproduces the transaction hash Koios claims, blake2b-256 over the auxiliary data equals transaction body key 7, and transaction body key 9 names the subject's policy id and asset name.

Those three establish self-consistency and that the metadata is bound to that transaction. They do not establish that the transaction was ever accepted into a block: anyone can construct bytes that never were. Reading the block out of the user's own immutable database is what closes that, and nothing smaller does.

The transaction id is blake2b-256 over the body as originally encoded. A CBOR library's canonical mode produced the wrong hash and its default encoding produced the right one, so the decoder must be able to hand back the original byte range of a decoded item. Check the candidate library for that before adopting it.

Blocks newer than k from the tip live in volatile/ and are not in the immutable database. On mainnet k is 2160 blocks at roughly 20 seconds average block time, so the window is on the order of 12 hours. Treat a pointer inside it as unresolved-for-now rather than as a failure: write asset_resolution in state 'pending' with a retry_after inside that window, and let the subject resolve on a later demand. This matters more than it sounds, because a freshly minted asset is exactly the one a user has just acquired and most wants to see named, so the common case for an NFT is the one that resolves late. Reading volatile/ as well would close it and is explicitly not in this task's scope; if that is wanted, it is its own task against a different on-disk format.

Auxiliary data has three historical shapes: a bare metadata map in Shelley, a two-element array in Allegra and Mary, and from Alonzo a CBOR tag 259 map whose key 0 holds the metadata, with the CIP-25 721 payload two levels down inside the tag.
This runs in the main process. It is file I O plus CBOR decoding and needs no Rust and no protocol library.
Immutable chunk layout is an undocumented internal format. Record the version it was read against and fail closed on a shape it does not recognize rather than guessing.

Name the CBOR decoder in this task rather than in an acceptance criterion. The confirmation needs a decoder that hands back the original byte range of a decoded item, because the transaction id is blake2b-256 over the body as originally encoded and a canonical re-encode produces the wrong hash. Neither cbor@5.2.0 nor borc@2.1.2 exposes that. Choosing one is a PRD-level decision about the 'no new runtime dependency' requirement and belongs on the record before the work starts.

CBOR decoder, settled: no new runtime dependency. source/main/assets/cborSpan.ts is a structural reader that returns byte ranges rather than values, because the byte-range requirement is real and neither cbor@5.0.2 nor borc@2.1.2 meets it. It is not a decoder, its failure mode is one-directional because every use sits inside a check whose failure writes no row, and ranges are needed in three places rather than one. This closes PRD open question 2.

The volatile window is measured against the immutable database's own tip rather than against k and a slot length. The tip is the last entry of the highest chunk, which needs no per-network constant and answers exactly the question being asked: does this database hold that slot yet.
The chunk size is derived from chunk zero's primary index, whose length is chunkSize + 2 offsets, rather than hardcoded per network.

The mint check reads the quantity. The recorded transaction mints one asset and burns another under the same policy in the same field, so a check that only matched the key would confirm the burned one.

Verified end to end on 2026-09-16 against the 17 GiB preprod immutable database on the development machine and a live tx_cbor response: chunk size derived as 21600, tip slot 131566495, pointer confirmed and the CIP-25 name extracted. That run is evidence rather than a committed test, because CI has no chain.

tasks.title: Ingest CIP-25 and CIP-68 as chain-sourced rows, and render their names
tasks.description: Write the confirmed record into asset_metadata with source = 'chain', the mint block's absolute_slot in slot, sequence_number NULL, decimals NULL and verified = 0, and extend the name resolution order so a CIP-25 or CIP-68 name renders below the registry name and above the decoded asset name.
implementationNotes: decimals stays NULL on every chain row. That is the mechanical form of PRD locked decision 10: verified decimal places come only from tokens.cardano.org, and no amount anywhere is formatted by a number that came from Koios.
verified stays 0 on every chain row. verified means the registry verification chain passed, and a chain row never runs it, so it never claims it.

One row per subject. The chain channel is consulted only for subjects the registry does not answer, and where both could answer the registry row stands, because it is the only one of the two that can carry verified decimals. This is a precedence rule in the resolver, not a schema change.
The CIP-25 or CIP-68 payload goes into the metadata JSON column as returned. Name resolution reads it; nothing else does.
A CIP-25 or CIP-68 image is a URI, usually ipfs://, not inline bytes. Store the URI in metadata and fetch nothing. An IPFS gateway is a further external dependency and is not in scope.
Where Koios answers with both cip68_metadata and minting_tx_metadata for a subject, the CIP-68 datum is the live record and is the one stored.

CIP-68 sits on weaker footing than CIP-25 and the code should say so in a comment: a CIP-68 datum lives at a spendable UTxO, so the mint transaction says nothing about its current value, and confirming it locally would mean a local-state-query against the node, which this plan does not build. It is acceptable because a CIP-68 value here supplies a name and nothing else.
Name order in Asset.tsx: registry ticker, registry name, chain name, decoded asset name when printable, nothing.

Precedence is enforced by not asking: a subject with a registry row is excluded before the pointer request, so no chain row is ever built for it and the question of which write wins never arises. That is also the filter the privacy argument depends on, because the registry answers for fungible holdings and they therefore never reach the index.

The selected pointer source travels on the existing metadata request rather than on a channel of its own. The setting lives in the renderer and the client in the main process, and one field cannot fall out of step.

A chain name is not marked minter-chosen. It is in the transaction that minted the asset, which had to satisfy the minting policy, so it is bound to that policy; a decoded asset name is bound to nothing, which is what the marker exists for.

tasks.title: Per-channel freshness: a closed policy freezes CIP-25 and nothing else
tasks.description: Apply the tiering the PRD already records. A registry row takes the seven-day window. A CIP-25 row under a closed policy is fetched once and never re-read. A CIP-68 row takes the seven-day window because a datum changes whenever its UTxO is spent.
implementationNotes: Closure is read from the policy script already in hand, not stored in a column of its own. The two-byte era wrapper says whether a lock can be expressed at all, and invalid_hereafter says whether it has passed.

Of 4,578 registry entries carrying a parseable policy, 4,104 (89.6 percent) are already closed, 47 close at a known future slot, and 427 (9.3 percent) are Shelley 8200-wrapped MultiSig scripts that cannot express a lock at all. That is what makes one resolution per asset for the life of an installation the realistic volume.

Plutus minting policies cannot be classified this way, because future behavior is not statically determinable. Treat an unclassifiable policy as open and apply the seven-day window. Do not assume the Plutus share is small; it is unmeasured.
Closure does not freeze the registry record. The attestation key still exists and can still sign long after the minting window shuts, so a registry row never inherits a CIP-25 row's permanence.

tasks.notes: The failing-pointer case is the one worth doing by hand, because it is the check that makes the index untrusted by construction.

riskAreas: The registry attestation payload construction is not reproduced from first principles. A local sweep of 3,600 plausible constructions against a real mainnet subject did not match the published signature, so it is read from the registry's own implementation and confirmed by the corpus gate in task-009 rather than by inspection.

Ed25519 verification must be strict, because verified decimal places change a displayed and entered amount. Node's built-in crypto.verify is used rather than cardano-crypto.js, which accepts a signature whose scalar S has had the group order added to it. If Node's verifier turns out not to be strict enough on some platform build, @noble/curves is promoted from a transitive dependency to a declared one; the primitive sits behind one module so nothing else changes.

task-002 is a live defect that the current poll masks. Landing the cache without it would empty the send form, the send confirmation and the transaction list on a cold start, because getNonZeroAssetTokens filters on an identity it takes from the cache rather than from the token.

task-003 is a live input-validation defect today, independent of this plan. An asset whose decimal places the user has never set accepts a decimal separator and then has it stripped by string substitution, so 1.5 becomes 15 natural units. Severity is bounded: ledger quantities are integers and decimals are presentation, so the harm is a large underpayment by the user's own hand, not an unintended overspend. Normal bug, not an emergency.
Dropping the assets endpoint also drops the only source of the CIP-14 fingerprint the token row renders as its primary identifier. task-005 must land before task-018 or every row loses its identity.

node:sqlite is used without a native module, which is the point, but it is the first use of it in this repository. It is confirmed present in Electron 41.3.0 on Node 24.15.0 with STRICT tables, CHECK constraints and WAL all working, and a future Electron bump should re-run that probe.

Registry logos are large: a 36,191 byte median entry and 316 MiB across the corpus. The volume bound is at the transport, because the bulk query never requests the logo property, and the store bounds are a second line rather than the first.

The migration in task-021 is where the overspend direction lives. Applying verified decimals moves no balance, but the send field flips from raw units to issuer units at the same moment: a user who types 1500000 from habit after the change sends a million and a half tokens instead of one and a half, gated only by their balance. The care belongs on the input path and its label, not on a balance notice, and the send confirmation is a partial backstop rather than a sufficient one.

Koios is adopted (PRD locked decision 9) and it is additive to tokens.cardano.org, never a replacement (locked decision 10). This is the risk most likely to be misread later, because the two sources overlap in what they return and not in what they prove: Koios strips the registry signatures, so a row taking its decimals from Koios would mean verified collapses to the server said so. The structural guard is in task-035, where a chain row is written with decimals NULL and verified 0, and in task-037, which asserts that shape so a later change cannot quietly route Koios decimals into the formatter.

Freshness is per channel, not per asset, and the plan now stores all three. A closed policy freezes minting and therefore CIP-25, which lives in the mint transaction; it does not freeze the registry record, because the attestation key still exists and can still sign after the minting window shuts; and it does not freeze CIP-68, which lives in a spendable datum. Of 4,578 entries carrying a parseable policy, 4,104 (89.6 percent) are already closed, 47 close at a known future slot, and 427 (9.3 percent) are Shelley 8200-wrapped MultiSig scripts that cannot express a lock at all. Plutus policies cannot be classified this way and the measured corpus is native-script only, so an unclassifiable policy is treated as open. Closure is read from the policy script already in hand rather than stored in a column of its own.

CIP-68 is stored on weaker footing than CIP-25 and the difference must stay visible. A CIP-25 payload is in the mint transaction, so the local block read in task-034 confirms it. A CIP-68 payload is a datum at a spendable UTxO, so the mint transaction says nothing about its current value, and confirming it locally would mean a local-state-query against the node, which this plan does not build. It is acceptable only because a CIP-68 value here supplies a name and nothing else, which is the class of risk locked decision 5 already accepts for an unverified registry name.

task-034 reads the immutable chunk format, which is an undocumented internal format and the fragile part of phase 7. It fails closed on a shape it does not recognize rather than guessing, and blocks newer than k from the tip are not in it at all, so a very recent mint resolves on a later demand rather than erroring. A node bump is a reason to re-run that reader against a real chain.

The direct option is in the settings enum from task-030 and is not built. A mint-field scan was measured at 48 to 58 seconds across the local preprod immutable database, 15.64 GiB across 6,092 chunks, on 2026-09-11. Mainnet is not synced on that machine, so the mainnet figures are extrapolation from that preprod measurement and not measurement: roughly 9 to 11 minutes on the same fast disk and an estimated 31 to 61 minutes on a modest or contended one, once. It is a mint-field traversal rather than a full decode, which is why it sits far below a full-chain decode estimate. securityNotes: verified is computed in the main process and never carried from the wire. No field of the registry response sets it.

The boolean collapses three classes into two. Policy-bound is true; signed with a key the policy does not require, and unattested, are both false. Only the policy-bound case justifies changing a displayed balance without asking, because an operator who can sign with an unbound key can assert any decimal places they like.

Verification gates decimal places only. A ticker or a name that fails verification is still shown: the worst case of a wrong name is a confusing label, and the worst case of a wrong decimal count is a transaction for the wrong amount.

One advisory, in one place. A wallet that decorates every token with security chrome trains its users to ignore chrome, and a large share of registry subjects carry no policy field at all, so a per-row badge would appear on most rows.

verified proves that the policy which minted the token authored the metadata. It proves nothing about which token this is: 660 registry tickers collide across 4,256 subjects, 53 percent of the corpus, many of them fully policy-bound, so two policies can both verify while both claiming one ticker. Anyone can mint a policy and sign metadata claiming any ticker. The cache stores the ticker, so implementers need to know that limit, but choosing between claimants is a trust-surface problem handled in the dApp connector security work and is out of scope here.

Koios is read as an index, not an oracle. A chain-sourced row is written only after the transaction the pointer names has been read out of the user's own immutable database and checked to mint that asset under that policy and to carry that metadata. An index that lies fails that check; an index that is unreachable leaves the row absent rather than wrong.

A chain row carries decimals NULL and verified 0. verified means the registry verification chain passed, and a chain row never runs it, so it never claims it. No amount anywhere is formatted by a number that came from Koios.

A user-supplied metadata source URL is checked against a pattern and then against a live probe of /tip before it is stored, which is what checkSmashServerHealth does for a user-supplied SMASH URL. An instance whose tip is far behind the user's own node is refused rather than accepted on a bare 200.
